claim: OsWRKY70 transcript levels increased rapidly following mechanical wounding in rice plants.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR analysis revealed low constitutive expression of OsWRKY70. Mechanical wounding and infestation by the rice striped stem borer (SSB) Chilo suppressalis resulted in a rapid increase in transcript levels (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data presented in Figure 1B showing increased transcript levels after mechanical wounding.

claim: OsWRKY70 transcript levels increased rapidly following infestation by Chilo suppressalis in rice plants.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR analysis revealed low constitutive expression of OsWRKY70. Mechanical wounding and infestation by the rice striped stem borer (SSB) Chilo suppressalis resulted in a rapid increase in transcript levels (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data presented in Figure 1A showing increased transcript levels after SSB infestation.

claim: Infestation by Nilaparvata lugens only slightly increased OsWRKY70 transcription levels.
source: Infestation by the rice brown planthopper (BPH) Nilaparvata lugens only slightly increased the transcription levels of (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data presented in Figure 1C showing minimal increase in transcript levels after BPH infestation.

claim: JA treatment did not induce OsWRKY70 expression.
source: JA or SA treatment did not induce OsWRKY70 (Figure 1D), suggesting that OsWRKY70 is an early regulator of plant responses to herbivores.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data presented in Figure 1D showing no induction after JA treatment.

claim: SA treatment did not induce OsWRKY70 expression.
source: JA or SA treatment did not induce OsWRKY70 (Figure 1D), suggesting that OsWRKY70 is an early regulator of plant responses to herbivores.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data presented in Figure 1D showing no induction after SA treatment.

claim: OsWRKY70 is an early regulator of plant responses to herbivores.
source: JA or SA treatment did not induce OsWRKY70 (Figure 1D), suggesting that OsWRKY70 is an early regulator of plant responses to herbivores.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OsWRKY70 is not induced by hormones but is induced by herbivores, placing it upstream of hormonal signaling.

claim: OsWRKY70 is exclusively localized in the nucleus.
source: Fluorescence analysis showed that OsWRKY70 is exclusively localized in the nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing nuclear localization of OsWRKY70:GFP fusion protein.

claim: OsWRKY70 recombinant protein specifically binds to the conserved W-box.
source: These results indicated that the recombinant OsWRKY70 protein specifically binds to the conserved W-box in the synthesized probe.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA assays showing specific binding to W-box sequences and loss of binding with mutated W-box.

claim: OsWRKY70 functions as a transcriptional activator in the yeast system.
source: OsWRKY70 is therefore likely functioning as a transcriptional activator in the yeast system.
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast one-hybrid assay showing blue color development indicating transcriptional activation activity.

claim: The promoter region of WRKY70 contains four W-boxes upstream of the transcription start site.
source: We found that the promoter region of WRKY70 contains four W-boxes, three reverse W-boxes (AGTCAA at −82 to −77, AGTCAA at −56 to −51, and GGTCAA at −49 to −44), and one forward W-box (TTGACC at −62 to −57), upstream of the transcription start site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of the WRKY70 promoter region.

claim: WRKY70 can self-activate its transcription.
source: Using WRKY70 promoter:GUS as a reporter and 35S: WRKY70-GFP, 35S:GFP as effectors expressed transiently in N. benthamiana, we found that WRKY70-GFP significantly increased the GUS activities compared to GFP alone, suggesting that WRKY70 can self-activate its transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transient expression assays showing increased GUS activity when WRKY70 is co-expressed with its own promoter.

claim: OsWRKY70 has four SP clusters in the N-terminal region.
source: OsWRKY70 has four SP clusters in the N-terminal region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but has no D domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: OsWRKY70 has no D domains.
source: OsWRKY70 has four SP clusters in the N-terminal region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but has no D domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of OsWRKY70.

claim: OsWRKY70 can interact with OsMPK3 in vitro.
source: OsWRKY70-His was pulled down strongly by GST-MPK3 and mildly by GST-MPK6, suggesting that OsWRKY70 can interact with both OsMPK3 and OsMPK6, with the OsWRKY70–OsMPK3 interaction being more efficient than the OsWRKY70–OsMPK6 interaction in vitro (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data showing interaction between OsWRKY70 and OsMPK3.

claim: OsWRKY70 can interact with OsMPK6 in vitro.
source: OsWRKY70-His was pulled down strongly by GST-MPK3 and mildly by GST-MPK6, suggesting that OsWRKY70 can interact with both OsMPK3 and OsMPK6, with the OsWRKY70–OsMPK3 interaction being more efficient than the OsWRKY70–OsMPK6 interaction in vitro (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data showing interaction between OsWRKY70 and OsMPK6.

claim: The OsWRKY70–OsMPK3 interaction is more efficient than the OsWRKY70–OsMPK6 interaction in vitro.
source: OsWRKY70-His was pulled down strongly by GST-MPK3 and mildly by GST-MPK6, suggesting that OsWRKY70 can interact with both OsMPK3 and OsMPK6, with the OsWRKY70–OsMPK3 interaction being more efficient than the OsWRKY70–OsMPK6 interaction in vitro (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data showing stronger pull-down with OsMPK3 compared to OsMPK6.

claim: OsMPK3 physically interacts with OsWRKY70 in vivo.
source: Fluorescence was observed when nYFP-OsWRKY70 was co-injected with OsMPK3-cYFP or OsMPK6-cYFP, and the signals were in the nuclear compartment according to 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining. No fluorescence was observed when nYFP-OsWRKY70 was co-expressed with unfused cYFP (Figure 2C). Taken together, these results strongly suggest that OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 physically interact with OsWRKY70.
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC assay showing fluorescence complementation when OsWRKY70 and OsMPK3 are co-expressed.

claim: OsMPK6 physically interacts with OsWRKY70 in vivo.
source: Fluorescence was observed when nYFP-OsWRKY70 was co-injected with OsMPK3-cYFP or OsMPK6-cYFP, and the signals were in the nuclear compartment according to 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining. No fluorescence was observed when nYFP-OsWRKY70 was co-expressed with unfused cYFP (Figure 2C). Taken together, these results strongly suggest that OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 physically interact with OsWRKY70.
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC assay showing fluorescence complementation when OsWRKY70 and OsMPK6 are co-expressed.

claim: OsWRKY70 can be phosphorylated by OsMPK3.
source: The result showed that OsWRKY70 can be phosphorylated by both OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay using Phos-tag detection.

claim: OsWRKY70 can be phosphorylated by OsMPK6.
source: The result showed that OsWRKY70 can be phosphorylated by both OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay using Phos-tag detection.

claim: Phosphorylation does not alter the W-box-binding activity of OsWRKY70.
source: Moreover, an EMSA assay revealed that phosphorylation did not alter the W-box-binding activity of OsWRKY70 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA assays comparing binding activity of phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated OsWRKY70.

claim: Phosphorylation of OsWRKY70 increases its transactivation activity.
source: GUS activity was higher in OsMKK4DD-MPK3-OsWRKY70 or OsMKK4DD-MPK6-OsWRKY70 co-expressed leaves than leaves expressing OsWRKY70 alone (Figure 2E). These results show that phosphorylation of OsWRKY70 can increase transactivation activity, but not W-box binding activity, of OsWRKY70.
evidence: The claim is supported by transient expression assays showing increased GUS activity when OsWRKY70 is co-expressed with activated MAPKs.

claim: OsWRKY70 transcript levels were significantly decreased in OsMPK3 silenced lines after SSB infestation.
source: OsWRKY70 transcript levels were significantly decreased in OsMPK3 (Wang et al., 2013) and OsMPK6 silenced lines (Figure 3A) after infestation with SSB for 1 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing reduced OsWRKY70 expression in OsMPK3 silenced lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 transcript levels were significantly decreased in OsMPK6 silenced lines after SSB infestation.
source: OsWRKY70 transcript levels were significantly decreased in OsMPK3 (Wang et al., 2013) and OsMPK6 silenced lines (Figure 3A) after infestation with SSB for 1 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing reduced OsWRKY70 expression in OsMPK6 silenced lines.

claim: OsWRKY24 was down-regulated in OsMPK6 silenced plants after SSB infestation.
source: Another group I-type WRKY TF, OsWRKY24, which has both SP clusters and a D domain, was down-regulated in OsMPK6 silenced plants, but not in OsMPK3 silenced lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing reduced OsWRKY24 expression in OsMPK6 silenced lines.

claim: OsWRKY24 was not down-regulated in OsMPK3 silenced plants after SSB infestation.
source: Another group I-type WRKY TF, OsWRKY24, which has both SP clusters and a D domain, was down-regulated in OsMPK6 silenced plants, but not in OsMPK3 silenced lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing no change in OsWRKY24 expression in OsMPK3 silenced lines.

claim: OsMPK3 transcript levels in WRKY70 silenced lines were the same as in wild-type plants after SSB infestation.
source: In WRKY70 silenced lines (see below) on the other hand, OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 transcripts were the same as in wild-type (WT) plants (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing no difference in OsMPK3 expression between WRKY70 silenced and WT plants.

claim: OsMPK6 transcript levels in WRKY70 silenced lines were the same as in wild-type plants after SSB infestation.
source: In WRKY70 silenced lines (see below) on the other hand, OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 transcripts were the same as in wild-type (WT) plants (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing no difference in OsMPK6 expression between WRKY70 silenced and WT plants.

claim: The transcript levels of OsWRKY70 are regulated by OsMPK3 and OsMPK6.
source: These results show that the transcript levels of OsWRKY70 is regulated by OsMPK3 and OsMPK6, but not vice versa.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing reduced OsWRKY70 expression in MAPK silenced lines but no change in MAPK expression in WRKY70 silenced lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 overexpression resulted in dwarfed plants.
source: OsWRKY70 overexpression resulted in dwarfed plants (Figure 4B), suggesting that OsWRKY70 is a negative growth regulator.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations of overexpression lines showing reduced plant height.

claim: OsWRKY70 is a negative growth regulator.
source: OsWRKY70 overexpression resulted in dwarfed plants (Figure 4B), suggesting that OsWRKY70 is a negative growth regulator.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that overexpression of OsWRKY70 causes dwarfism.

claim: Hemizygous oeWRKY70 lines displayed dark green leaves and delayed flowering.
source: In soil, the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines displayed dark green leaves and delayed flowering, similar to known GA-deficient mutants (Sakamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations of hemizygous overexpression lines and comparison to known GA-deficient mutants.

claim: Plant height was reduced by 29% and 27% in hemi-oeWRKY70-8 and hemi-oeWRKY70-17 lines, respectively.
source: Plant height was reduced by 29% and 27%, and root length by 49% and 30%, respectively (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of plant height in transgenic lines compared to WT.

claim: Root length was reduced by 49% and 30% in hemi-oeWRKY70-8 and hemi-oeWRKY70-17 lines, respectively.
source: Plant height was reduced by 29% and 27%, and root length by 49% and 30%, respectively (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of root length in transgenic lines compared to WT.

claim: GA1, GA7, GA19, GA20, GA24, and GA53 levels were significantly lower in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines than in WT plants.
source: The experiment revealed that GA1, GA7, GA19, GA20, GA24, and GA53 levels were significantly lower in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines (hemi-oeWRKY70-8 and hemi-oeWRKY70-17) than in WT plants (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC/MS-MS measurements of GA levels in transgenic lines.

claim: The growth phenotype of oeWRKY70 seedlings was successfully restored to WT levels when grown on 1/2 MS plates with GA3 at a concentration of 0.01 μM.
source: Moreover, the growth phenotype of the oeWRKY70 seedlings was successfully restored to WT levels when they were grown on 1/2 MS plates with GA3 at a concentration of 0.01 μM (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations of GA3-treated overexpression lines showing restored growth.

claim: GA20ox7 was significantly down-regulated in the hemi-oeWRKY70-8 lines.
source: Consistently, the GA biosynthesis gene GA 20 oxidase (GA20ox7) was significantly down-regulated in the hemi-oeWRKY70-8 lines (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing reduced GA20ox7 expression in overexpression lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 regulates plant growth through GA biosynthesis.
source: These results suggest that OsWRKY70 regulates plant growth through GA biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including reduced GA levels, down-regulation of GA biosynthesis genes, and GA complementation experiments.

claim: JA levels in irWRKY70 lines were significantly decreased compared with WT plants upon SSB attack.
source: JA levels in the irWRKY70 lines were significantly decreased compared with WT plants upon SSB attack, while they were increased in the overexpressing lines (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS measurements of JA levels in transgenic lines after SSB infestation.

claim: JA levels were increased in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines upon SSB attack.
source: JA levels in the irWRKY70 lines were significantly decreased compared with WT plants upon SSB attack, while they were increased in the overexpressing lines (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS measurements of JA levels in transgenic lines after SSB infestation.

claim: OsWRKY70 positively regulated SSB-induced transcript levels of OsHI-LOX.
source: In accordance with this data OsWRKY70 positively regulated SSB-induced transcript levels of the JA-biosynthesis genes OsHI-LOX (Zhou et al., 2009) and OsAOS2 (Mei et al., 2006) (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing altered OsHI-LOX expression in WRKY70 transgenic lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 positively regulated SSB-induced transcript levels of OsAOS2.
source: In accordance with this data OsWRKY70 positively regulated SSB-induced transcript levels of the JA-biosynthesis genes OsHI-LOX (Zhou et al., 2009) and OsAOS2 (Mei et al., 2006) (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing altered OsAOS2 expression in WRKY70 transgenic lines.

claim: Ethylene accumulation was similar in irWRKY70 lines and WT plants after SSB infestation.
source: The accumulation of ethylene was similar in the irWRKY70 lines and WT plants, but the levels were significantly elevated in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines after SSB infestation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ethylene measurements showing no difference between irWRKY70 and WT plants.

claim: Ethylene levels were significantly elevated in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines after SSB infestation.
source: The accumulation of ethylene was similar in the irWRKY70 lines and WT plants, but the levels were significantly elevated in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines after SSB infestation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ethylene measurements showing increased levels in overexpression lines.

claim: Transcript levels of OsACS2 were similar in irWRKY70 and WT plants when infested by SSB.
source: Consistent with this result, transcript levels of the ethylene biosynthesis gene OsACS2 were similar in irWRKY70 and WT plants when infested by SSB, but were much higher in the induced hemi-oeWRKY70 lines (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing no difference in OsACS2 expression between irWRKY70 and WT plants.

claim: Transcript levels of OsACS2 were much higher in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines after SSB infestation.
source: Consistent with this result, transcript levels of the ethylene biosynthesis gene OsACS2 were similar in irWRKY70 and WT plants when infested by SSB, but were much higher in the induced hemi-oeWRKY70 lines (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing increased OsACS2 expression in overexpression lines.

claim: WT plants and irWRKY70 lines had nearly identical constitutive and SSB-induced SA levels.
source: WT plants and irWRKY70 lines had nearly identical constitutive and SSB-induced SA levels, whereas the SA levels in the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines were significantly lower than in WT plants (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS measurements of SA levels showing no difference between irWRKY70 and WT plants.

claim: SA levels in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines were significantly lower than in WT plants.
source: WT plants and irWRKY70 lines had nearly identical constitutive and SSB-induced SA levels, whereas the SA levels in the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines were significantly lower than in WT plants (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS measurements of SA levels showing reduced levels in overexpression lines.

claim: OsICS1 transcriptional level was significantly decreased in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines compared with WT plants after SSB infestation.
source: We examined the OsICS1 gene (Du et al., 2009) in rice after SSB infestation and found that the OsICS1 transcriptional level was significantly decreased in the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines compared with WT plants (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing reduced OsICS1 expression in overexpression lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 positively regulates SSB-induced JA levels.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that OsWRKY70 positively regulates SSB-induced JA- and ET levels but negatively regulates SA levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by hormone measurements showing increased JA in overexpression lines and decreased JA in silenced lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 positively regulates SSB-induced ET levels.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that OsWRKY70 positively regulates SSB-induced JA- and ET levels but negatively regulates SA levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by hormone measurements showing increased ET in overexpression lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 negatively regulates SSB-induced SA levels.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that OsWRKY70 positively regulates SSB-induced JA- and ET levels but negatively regulates SA levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by hormone measurements showing decreased SA in overexpression lines.

claim: The levels of constitutive and SSB-induced OsWRKY70 transcripts in as-lox plants were the same as those in WT plants over the first 60 min of infestation.
source: The experiments revealed that the levels of constitutive and SSB-induced OsWRKY70 transcripts in as-lox and as-acs plants were the same as those in WT plants over the first 60 min of infestation (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that OsWRKY70 functions upstream of JA and ET signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing no difference in OsWRKY70 expression between as-lox and WT plants.

claim: The levels of constitutive and SSB-induced OsWRKY70 transcripts in as-acs plants were the same as those in WT plants over the first 60 min of infestation.
source: The experiments revealed that the levels of constitutive and SSB-induced OsWRKY70 transcripts in as-lox and as-acs plants were the same as those in WT plants over the first 60 min of infestation (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that OsWRKY70 functions upstream of JA and ET signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing no difference in OsWRKY70 expression between as-acs and WT plants.

claim: OsWRKY70 functions upstream of JA and ET signaling.
source: The experiments revealed that the levels of constitutive and SSB-induced OsWRKY70 transcripts in as-lox and as-acs plants were the same as those in WT plants over the first 60 min of infestation (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that OsWRKY70 functions upstream of JA and ET signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that JA and ET biosynthesis mutants do not affect OsWRKY70 expression.

claim: TrypPI activity was suppressed in irWRKY70 lines compared with WT plants.
source: TrypPI activity was suppressed in the irWRKY70 lines and enhanced in the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines compared with WT plants (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TrypPI activity assays showing reduced activity in silenced lines.

claim: TrypPI activity was enhanced in hemi-oeWRKY70 lines compared with WT plants.
source: TrypPI activity was suppressed in the irWRKY70 lines and enhanced in the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines compared with WT plants (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TrypPI activity assays showing increased activity in overexpression lines.

claim: SSB caterpillars gained more mass on irWRKY70 plants compared to those fed on WT plants.
source: As expected, SSB caterpillars gained more mass on irWRKY70-7 and irWRKY70-8 plants and less mass on the overexpressing lines compared to those fed on WT plants (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by larval mass measurements showing increased mass on silenced lines.

claim: SSB caterpillars gained less mass on hemi-oeWRKY70 plants compared to those fed on WT plants.
source: As expected, SSB caterpillars gained more mass on irWRKY70-7 and irWRKY70-8 plants and less mass on the overexpressing lines compared to those fed on WT plants (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by larval mass measurements showing decreased mass on overexpression lines.

claim: IrWRKY70 lines were more severely damaged by SSB than WT plants.
source: IrWRKY70 lines were more severely damaged by SSB than the WT plants, whereas the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines were less damaged (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observations of plant damage after SSB infestation.

claim: Hemi-oeWRKY70 lines were less damaged by SSB than WT plants.
source: IrWRKY70 lines were more severely damaged by SSB than the WT plants, whereas the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines were less damaged (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observations of plant damage after SSB infestation.

claim: JA treatment attenuated the difference in TrypPI levels between WT plants and irWRKY70 lines.
source: JA treatment attenuated the difference in TrypPI levels between WT plants and the irWRKY70 lines (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by TrypPI activity assays after JA treatment showing restored levels in silenced lines.

claim: SSB larvae fed on JA-treated irWRKY70 lines gained a similar amount of weight to those fed on equally treated WT plants.
source: Moreover, SSB larvae fed on JA-treated irWRKY70 lines gained a similar amount of weight to those fed on equally treated WT plants (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by larval mass measurements after JA treatment showing no difference between silenced and WT lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 mediates rice-resistance to SSB through JA signaling.
source: The complete restoration of plant resistance to SSB and elicited accumulation of TrypPIs in irWRKY70 by exogenous JA application suggests that OsWRKY70 mediates rice-resistance to SSB through JA signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by JA complementation experiments showing restored resistance in silenced lines.

claim: BPH adult females preferred feeding on WT plants rather than irWRKY70 lines.
source: When irWRKY70 lines and WT plants were exposed to a BPH colony, adult females preferred feeding on the WT rather than the irWRKY70 lines (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by choice assays showing fewer BPH on silenced lines compared to WT.

claim: BPH adult females laid more eggs on WT plants than irWRKY70 lines.
source: Similarly, BPH adult females laid more eggs on WT plants than irWRKY70 (Figure 8A,B, inserts).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg counts showing more eggs on WT plants compared to silenced lines.

claim: BPH adult females were found more often on hemi-oeWRKY70 lines than on WT plants.
source: In accordance with these findings, BPH adult females were found more often on hemi-oeWRKY70 lines than on WT plants and laid more eggs on the former than on the latter (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by choice assays showing more BPH on overexpression lines compared to WT.

claim: BPH adult females laid more eggs on hemi-oeWRKY70 lines than on WT plants.
source: In accordance with these findings, BPH adult females were found more often on hemi-oeWRKY70 lines than on WT plants and laid more eggs on the former than on the latter (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg counts showing more eggs on overexpression lines compared to WT.

claim: BPH nymphs fed on irWRKY70 lines had lower survival rates than those fed on WT plants.
source: Moreover, BPH nymphs fed on the irWRKY70 lines had lower survival rates than those fed on WT plants; in contrast, BPH nymphs fed on the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines had higher survival rates (Figure 8E,F), showing that OsWRKY70 negatively regulates rice BPH resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate measurements showing lower survival on silenced lines.

claim: BPH nymphs fed on hemi-oeWRKY70 lines had higher survival rates than those fed on WT plants.
source: Moreover, BPH nymphs fed on the irWRKY70 lines had lower survival rates than those fed on WT plants; in contrast, BPH nymphs fed on the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines had higher survival rates (Figure 8E,F), showing that OsWRKY70 negatively regulates rice BPH resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate measurements showing higher survival on overexpression lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 negatively regulates rice BPH resistance.
source: Moreover, BPH nymphs fed on the irWRKY70 lines had lower survival rates than those fed on WT plants; in contrast, BPH nymphs fed on the hemi-oeWRKY70 lines had higher survival rates (Figure 8E,F), showing that OsWRKY70 negatively regulates rice BPH resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple BPH performance assays showing increased susceptibility in overexpression lines and increased resistance in silenced lines.

claim: BPH female adults preferred feeding on sd-1 mutant rather than WT (ZH11).
source: The BPH female adults preferred feeding and ovipositing on sd-1 rather than the WT (ZH11) (Figure 9A), whereas the eui lines repelled BPH feeding compared with WT plants and did not affect BPH oviposition (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by choice assays showing more BPH on sd-1 mutant compared to WT.

claim: BPH female adults preferred ovipositing on sd-1 mutant rather than WT (ZH11).
source: The BPH female adults preferred feeding and ovipositing on sd-1 rather than the WT (ZH11) (Figure 9A), whereas the eui lines repelled BPH feeding compared with WT plants and did not affect BPH oviposition (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg counts showing more eggs on sd-1 mutant compared to WT.

claim: The eui mutant repelled BPH feeding compared with WT plants.
source: The BPH female adults preferred feeding and ovipositing on sd-1 rather than the WT (ZH11) (Figure 9A), whereas the eui lines repelled BPH feeding compared with WT plants and did not affect BPH oviposition (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by choice assays showing fewer BPH on eui mutant compared to WT.

claim: The eui mutant did not affect BPH oviposition compared with WT plants.
source: The BPH female adults preferred feeding and ovipositing on sd-1 rather than the WT (ZH11) (Figure 9A), whereas the eui lines repelled BPH feeding compared with WT plants and did not affect BPH oviposition (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg counts showing no difference between eui mutant and WT.

claim: BPH nymph mortality was significantly higher on the eui mutant compared with WT plants.
source: The BPH nymph mortality was significant higher on the eui mutant compared with WT plants, but the sd-1 mutant did not influence BPH nymph performance (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate measurements showing lower survival on eui mutant.

claim: The sd-1 mutant did not influence BPH nymph performance.
source: The BPH nymph mortality was significant higher on the eui mutant compared with WT plants, but the sd-1 mutant did not influence BPH nymph performance (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate measurements showing no difference between sd-1 mutant and WT.

claim: GA3 application restored BPH resistance in hemi-oeWRKY70 mutants.
source: We found that GA3 application restored BPH resistance in hemi-oeWRKY70 mutants (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by BPH performance assays after GA3 treatment showing restored resistance in overexpression lines.

claim: BPH female adults showed no preference between WT and GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 lines for feeding.
source: Moreover, the GA-deficient mutant sd-1 improved the performance of BPH, whereas the GA-excessive mutant eui decreased BPH performance (Figure 9A–C). These data demonstrate that the GA-signaling pathway plays an important role in modulating resistance in rice to BPH in addition to its regulation of plant growth. GA-modulated BPH resistance in rice may occur via two mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by choice assays showing no difference between WT and GA3-treated overexpression lines.

claim: BPH female adults showed no preference between WT and GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 lines for oviposition.
source: BPH female adults feeding and ovipositing showed no preference between the WT and GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 lines (Figure 9D,E), and the BPH nymph survival rate was the same on GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 and WT plants (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg counts showing no difference between WT and GA3-treated overexpression lines.

claim: BPH nymph survival rate was the same on GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 and WT plants.
source: BPH female adults feeding and ovipositing showed no preference between the WT and GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 lines (Figure 9D,E), and the BPH nymph survival rate was the same on GA3-treated hemi-oeWRKY70 and WT plants (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate measurements showing no difference between WT and GA3-treated overexpression lines.

claim: The GA-signaling pathway plays an important role in modulating resistance in rice to BPH.
source: These data demonstrate that the GA-signaling pathway plays an important role in modulating resistance in rice to BPH in addition to its regulation of plant growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including GA mutant experiments and GA complementation experiments.

claim: Prioritizing defence over growth leads to a significant resistance trade-off.
source: Our study shows that prioritizing defence over growth leads to a significant resistance trade-off with important implications for the evolution and agricultural exploitation of plant immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that increasing resistance to SSB through OsWRKY70 increases susceptibility to BPH.

claim: Plants generally respond to herbivore attack by increasing resistance and decreasing growth.
source: Plants generally respond to herbivore attack by increasing resistance and decreasing growth.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about plant responses to herbivory.

claim: Defence prioritization is achieved through the regulation of phytohormonal signaling networks.
source: This prioritization is achieved through the regulation of phytohormonal signaling networks.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about plant hormone signaling.

claim: WRKY70 is a specific herbivore-induced, mitogen-activated protein kinase-regulated rice transcription factor.
source: In this study, we identify WRKY70 as a specific herbivore-induced, mitogen-activated protein kinase-regulated rice transcription factor that physically interacts with W-box motifs and prioritizes defence over growth by positively regulating jasmonic acid (JA) and negatively regulating gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis upon attack by the chewing herbivore Chilo suppressalis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing herbivore induction, MAPK regulation, and W-box binding.

claim: WRKY70 physically interacts with W-box motifs.
source: In this study, we identify WRKY70 as a specific herbivore-induced, mitogen-activated protein kinase-regulated rice transcription factor that physically interacts with W-box motifs and prioritizes defence over growth by positively regulating jasmonic acid (JA) and negatively regulating gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis upon attack by the chewing herbivore Chilo suppressalis.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA assays showing W-box binding.

claim: WRKY70 prioritizes defence over growth by positively regulating JA biosynthesis upon attack by Chilo suppressalis.
source: In this study, we identify WRKY70 as a specific herbivore-induced, mitogen-activated protein kinase-regulated rice transcription factor that physically interacts with W-box motifs and prioritizes defence over growth by positively regulating jasmonic acid (JA) and negatively regulating gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis upon attack by the chewing herbivore Chilo suppressalis.
evidence: The claim is supported by hormone measurements and gene expression data showing increased JA in overexpression lines.

claim: WRKY70 prioritizes defence over growth by negatively regulating GA biosynthesis upon attack by Chilo suppressalis.
source: In this study, we identify WRKY70 as a specific herbivore-induced, mitogen-activated protein kinase-regulated rice transcription factor that physically interacts with W-box motifs and prioritizes defence over growth by positively regulating jasmonic acid (JA) and negatively regulating gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis upon attack by the chewing herbivore Chilo suppressalis.
evidence: The claim is supported by hormone measurements and gene expression data showing decreased GA in overexpression lines.

claim: WRKY70-dependent JA biosynthesis is required for proteinase inhibitor activation.
source: WRKY70-dependent JA biosynthesis is required for proteinase inhibitor activation and resistance against C. suppressalis.
evidence: The claim is supported by TrypPI activity assays and JA complementation experiments.

claim: WRKY70-dependent JA biosynthesis is required for resistance against C. suppressalis.
source: WRKY70-dependent JA biosynthesis is required for proteinase inhibitor activation and resistance against C. suppressalis.
evidence: The claim is supported by herbivore performance assays and JA complementation experiments.

claim: WRKY70 induction increases plant susceptibility against Nilaparvata lugens.
source: In contrast, WRKY70 induction increases plant susceptibility against the rice brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens.
evidence: The claim is supported by BPH performance assays showing increased susceptibility in overexpression lines.

claim: WRKY70-dependent GA signaling is the causal factor in N. lugens susceptibility.
source: Experiments with GA-deficient rice lines identify WRKY70-dependent GA signaling as the causal factor in N. lugens susceptibility.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with GA mutants and GA complementation experiments.

claim: OsWRKY70 has two homologs in rice, OsWRKY24 and OsWRKY53, which share 53% and 51% amino acid sequence identity.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of group I-type WRKYs from different species revealed that OsWRKY70 has two homologs in rice, OsWRKY24 and OsWRKY53, which share 53% and 51% amino acid sequence identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and sequence comparison.

claim: OsWRKY70 belongs to group I WRKYs.
source: OsWRKY70 has two WRKY domains and belongs to group I (Rushton et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and classification according to established WRKY classification systems.

claim: OsWRKY70 has two WRKY domains.
source: OsWRKY70 has two WRKY domains and belongs to group I (Rushton et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of OsWRKY70.

claim: The full-length cDNA of OsWRKY70 includes an open reading frame of 1719 bp.
source: The full-length cDNA of the cloned OsWRKY, including an open reading frame (ORF) of 1719 bp, was obtained by reverse transcription PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular cloning and sequencing data.

claim: The cloned OsWRKY sequence was 100% identical to the previously identified OsWRKY70 (TIGR ID Os05g39720).
source: Blast analysis showed that the sequence was 100% identical to the previously identified OsWRKY70 (TIGR ID Os05g39720).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison using BLAST analysis.

claim: OsWRKY70 showed low constitutive expression.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR analysis revealed low constitutive expression of OsWRKY70.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing low expression in untreated plants.

claim: Plants have developed effective defensive systems to minimize herbivore damage.
source: Plants have developed effective defensive systems to minimize herbivore damage.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about plant defense systems.

claim: Plants can specifically perceive attackers and respond by activating defence-related signaling pathways.
source: They can specifically perceive attackers and respond to them by activating defence-related signaling pathways, including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades and hormone signaling, leading to the induction of numerous defence-related genes and defence compounds as well as plant resistance (Wu and Baldwin, 2010; Bonaventure et al., 2011; Erb et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: JA-, SA-, and ET-mediated signaling play a central role in induced resistance to herbivores.
source: Jasmonic acid (JA)-, salicylic acid (SA)-, and ethylene (ET)-mediated signaling play a central role in induced resistance to herbivores (Lu et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The induction of defences commonly co-occurs with a reduction of plant growth.
source: The induction of defences commonly co-occurs with a reduction of plant growth (Heinrich et al., 2013; Attaran et al., 2014; Huot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Plants actively prioritize defence over growth.
source: Through silencing defence-related genes, a direct negative link between defence and growth was demonstrated (Zavala and Baldwin, 2006; Zhang et al., 2008; Meldau et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012), suggesting that plants actively prioritize defence over growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from studies showing negative correlation between defense and growth when defense genes are silenced.

claim: Defence prioritization and associated growth trade-offs are regulated by crosstalk between plant hormones.
source: Defence prioritization and the associated growth trade-offs are regulated by crosstalk between plant hormones (Schwachtje et al., 2006; Stanton et al., 2013; Huot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DELLA proteins can physically interact with JAZ proteins, resulting in mutual suppression.
source: DELLA proteins for instance, which typically suppress gibberellin (GA) signaling, can physically interact with the JA pathway repressor JAZ proteins, thereby resulting in mutual suppression (Hou et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SA inhibits the expression of TIR1/ABF F-box genes, leading to stabilization of AUX/IAA repressor proteins and decreasing auxin signaling.
source: Furthermore, SA has been reported to inhibit the expression of TIR1/ABF F-box genes, thereby leading to stabilization of AUX/IAA repressor proteins and decreasing auxin signaling (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Auxin signaling can reduce SA biosynthesis and render plants more susceptible to pathogens.
source: Conversely, auxin signaling can reduce SA biosynthesis and thereby render plants more susceptible to pathogens (Robert–Seilaniantz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Little is known about the impact of growth-related hormones on herbivore resistance and potential resistance trade-offs.
source: Compared to the impact of defence-related hormones, little is known about the impact of growth-related hormones on herbivore resistance and potential resistance trade-offs that may emanate from prioritizing defence over growth through hormonal regulation (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Transcription factors play a potentially important role in herbivore-induced plant reconfiguration and defence prioritization.
source: Transcription factors (TFs) play a potentially important role in herbivore-induced plant reconfiguration and defence prioritization, as they regulate the expression of responses up and downstream of hormonal signaling pathways and thereby influence early and late signaling (Reymond et al., 2004; Dombrecht et al., 2007; Skibbe et al., 2008; Kaur et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2011; Schweizer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: AtMYC2 in Arabidopsis acts downstream of JA and regulates JA-dependent herbivore resistance.
source: AtMYC2 in Arabidopsis thaliana, for example, was reported to act downstream of JA and to regulate JA-dependent herbivore resistance (Dombrecht et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: MYC2, MYC3, and MYC4 regulate the production of toxic glucosinolates via direct transcriptional activation of glucosinolate biosynthesis genes.
source: Moreover, MYC2, MYC3, and MYC4 were shown to regulate the production of toxic glucosinolates via a direct transcriptional activation of glucosinolate biosynthesis genes (Schweizer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: NaMYB8 in Nicotiana attenuata modulates the accumulation of phenylpropanoid–polyamine conjugates, which are essential for defence against herbivores.
source: In Nicotiana attenuata, a R2R3-type MYB TF (NaMYB8) was found to modulate the accumulation of phenylpropanoid–polyamine conjugates, which are essential for defence against herbivores (Kaur et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OsERF3 functions as an early component upstream of MAPK signaling and modulates JA, SA, ET, and H2O2 levels as well as plant resistance to rice herbivores.
source: In rice, an EAR-motif-containing ERF TF (OsERF3) functions as an early component upstream of MAPK signaling and modulates JA, SA, ET, and H2O2 levels as well as plant resistance to rice herbivores (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Several WRKYs have been directly associated with defence against herbivores.
source: Also, several WRKYs, such as rice OsWRKY89, wheat TaWRKY53, Arabidopsis AtWRKY72, and tomato SIWRKY70 and SIWRKY72, have been directly associated with defence against herbivores (Wang et al., 2007; Bhattarai et al., 2010; Van Eck et al., 2010; Atamian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NaWRKY3 and NaWRKY6 in N. attenuata modulate elicited JA and JA-Ile/-Leu levels and mediate herbivory-induced defence responses.
source: NaWRKY3 and NaWRKY6 in N. attenuata have been shown to modulate elicited JA and JA-Ile/-Leu levels and thus mediate herbivory-induced defence responses (Skibbe et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Understanding of the consequences of defence prioritization for plant resistance has remained limited.
source: Identifying and manipulating TFs that are involved in defence prioritization would make it possible to assess the biological impact of herbivore-induced growth suppression. Yet, to date, such an approach has not been taken. Consequently, our understanding of the consequences of defence prioritization for plant resistance has remained limited.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Growth/defence and resistance trade-offs can emanate from the same mechanistic basis.
source: Our study reveals that growth/defence and resistance trade-offs can emanate from the same mechanistic basis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OsWRKY70 simultaneously affects growth, defense against SSB, and susceptibility to BPH.

claim: Reducing growth to support defence is more costly than previously anticipated from a plant's perspective.
source: From a plant's perspective, this suggests that reducing growth to support defence is even more costly than previously anticipated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that defense prioritization leads to both growth reduction and increased susceptibility to non-target herbivores.

claim: It may be problematic to breed resistant varieties that rely on induced defence.
source: From an agricultural point of view, this result indicates that it may be problematic to breed resistant varieties that rely on induced defence, as these plants may suffer from both a depression in growth and increased susceptibility to non-target herbivores.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that defense prioritization leads to trade-offs with implications for agriculture.

claim: OsWRKY70 is rapidly induced following mechanical wounding and SSB feeding, but not following attack by a piercing sucking herbivore.
source: OsWRKY70 is rapidly induced following mechanical wounding and SSB feeding, but not following attack by a piercing sucking herbivore.
evidence: The claim is supported by QRT-PCR data showing differential induction patterns.

claim: Group I-type WRKY TFs can be phosphorylated by MAPKs and the SP clusters are the phosphorylating sites.
source: It has been well documented that Group I-type WRKY TFs can be phosphorylated by MAPKs and that the SP clusters are the phosphorylating sites (Mao et al., 2011; Ishihama and Yoshioka, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Autoregulation and cross-regulation are common features of WRKY action.
source: Given that autoregulation and cross-regulation are common features of WRKY action (Ishihama and Yoshioka, 2012), OsWRKY70 transcript levels are likely reduced in OsMPK3 and 6 silenced lines because of the reduction in phosphorylated WRKY70 and other WRKYs, which decreases WRKY activity and thereby reduce OsWRKY70 transcript levels.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OsWRKY70 is at the interface between early recognition and signaling and hormonal regulation.
source: Combined with its capacity to bind to W-box sequences and to act as transcriptional activator, this places OsWRKY70 at the interface between early recognition and signaling and hormonal regulation (Rushton et al., 2010; Wu and Baldwin, 2010; Erb et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OsWRKY70 is regulated by MAPKs and regulates hormone biosynthesis.

claim: OsWRKY70 reduces plant growth and increases defence upon herbivore attack.
source: Indeed, silencing and over-expression of OsWRKY70 demonstrates its central role in regulating defence and growth through JA, ET, SA, and GA signaling, which enables OsWRKY70 to reduce plant growth and increases defence upon herbivore attack.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing altered growth and defense in transgenic lines.

claim: WRKYs play important roles in the regulation of transcriptional reprogramming associated with plant growth, development, and stress responses.
source: In other plant systems, WRKYs have also been reported to play important roles in the regulation of transcriptional reprogramming associated with plant growth, development, and stress responses at different levels, including upstream and downstream of protein kinases and hormones (Rushton et al., 2010; Ishihama et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NaWRKY3 and NaWRKY6 function downstream of NaSIPK and NaWIPK and upstream of JA biosynthesis.
source: NaWRKY3 and NaWRKY6, the homologs of OsWRKY70 in N. attenuata, for instance, have been reported to function downstream of NaSIPK and NaWIPK and upstream of JA biosynthesis (Skibbe et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: AtWRKY33 is phosphorylated by AtMPK3/MPK6 and can affect ET synthesis by directly binding promoter region of ACS2 and ACS6 genes.
source: In Arabidopsis, AtWRKY33, the homolog of OsWRKY70 is phosphorylated by AtMPK3/MPK6 and can affect ET synthesis by directly binding promoter region of ACS2 and ACS6 genes (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OsWRKY24 represses GA signaling in rice aleurone cells.
source: Another rice WRKY, OsWRKY24 has been reported to repress GA signaling in rice aleurone cells (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OsWRKY70 may directly bind to genes involved in hormone biosynthesis and signaling.
source: OsWRKY70 may regulate phytohormone signaling via two, not mutually exclusive routes. First, it may directly bind to genes that are involved in hormone biosynthesis and signaling.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the presence of W-box motifs in hormone biosynthesis gene promoters.

claim: The existence of W-box or W-box like motifs in the promoters of hormone biosynthesis genes provides indirect evidence for their interaction with OsWRKY70.
source: The existence of W-box or W-box like motifs in the promoters of these genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) provides additional indirect evidence for their interaction with OsWRKY70.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis showing W-box motifs in promoters.

claim: OsWRKY70 may regulate growth and defence through indirect hormonal cross-talk.
source: Second, OsWRKY may regulate growth and defence through indirect hormonal cross-talk.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known hormone crosstalk mechanisms.

claim: The JA-signaling pathway is connected to the GA-signaling pathway through COI1-JAZ1-DELLA-PIF complexes, resulting in mutual suppression.
source: It has been reported that the JA-signaling pathway is connected to the GA-signaling pathway through COI1-JAZ1-DELLA-PIF complexes, resulting in mutual suppression.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The activation of JA signaling inhibits GA-mediated plant growth.
source: The activation of JA signaling inhibits GA-mediated plant growth, whereas the activation of the GA pathway inhibits JA-mediated plant defence (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The activation of the GA pathway inhibits JA-mediated plant defence.
source: The activation of JA signaling inhibits GA-mediated plant growth, whereas the activation of the GA pathway inhibits JA-mediated plant defence (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: JA inhibits GA biosynthesis via an unknown mechanism.
source: Moreover, JA was found to inhibit GA biosynthesis via an unknown mechanism (Yang et al., 2012; Heinrich et al., 2013), and the GA-GID1-DELLA complex was found to positively regulate the production of SA (Navarro et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The GA-GID1-DELLA complex positively regulates the production of SA.
source: Moreover, JA was found to inhibit GA biosynthesis via an unknown mechanism (Yang et al., 2012; Heinrich et al., 2013), and the GA-GID1-DELLA complex was found to positively regulate the production of SA (Navarro et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The observed phytohormone levels and associated phenotypes in transgenic OsWRKY70 lines might be at least in part due to antagonistic and synergistic phytohormone crosstalk.
source: Thus, the observed phytohormone levels and associated phenotypes in the transgenic OsWRKY70 lines might be at least in part due to antagonistic and synergistic phytohormone crosstalk.
evidence: The claim is inferred from known hormone crosstalk mechanisms and observed phenotypes.

claim: The absence of JA signaling enhances the sensitivity of plants to GAs.
source: It has also been reported that the absence of JA signaling enhances the sensitivity of plants to GAs (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The promotion of JA signaling in oeWRKY70 lines did not decrease the sensitivity of plants to GA3.
source: In our experiments, the promotion of JA signaling in oeWRKY70 lines did not decrease the sensitivity of plants to GA3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by GA3 dose-response experiments.

claim: The dwarf phenotype of oeWRKY70 lines was completely restored by exogenous GA3 at low concentrations of 0.01 μM.
source: Moreover, the dwarf phenotype of oeWRKY70 lines was completely restored by exogenous GA3 at low concentrations of 0.01 μM (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations after GA3 treatment.

claim: The dwarf phenotype of oeWRKY70 lines is directly related to the low level of GAs.
source: This suggests that the dwarf phenotype of oeWRKY70 lines is directly related to the low level of GAs and that the sensitivity of plants to GAs may be influenced by other OsWRKY70-mediated factors other than JA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from GA complementation experiments.

claim: The sensitivity of plants to GAs may be influenced by other OsWRKY70-mediated factors other than JA.
source: This suggests that the dwarf phenotype of oeWRKY70 lines is directly related to the low level of GAs and that the sensitivity of plants to GAs may be influenced by other OsWRKY70-mediated factors other than JA.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observation that JA does not affect GA sensitivity in oeWRKY70 lines.

claim: GA levels are unlikely to be altered in irWRKY70 lines.
source: Interestingly, irWRKY70 lines showed similar growth phenotypes to WT plants, indicating that GA levels are unlikely to be altered in irWRKY70 lines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that irWRKY70 lines have normal growth.

claim: OsWRKY24 and OsWRKY53 may be involved in the biosynthesis of GAs.
source: This suggests an involvement of other factors, such as the homologs of OsWRKY70, OsWRKY24, and OsWRKY53, in the biosynthesis of GAs.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observation that irWRKY70 lines have normal GA levels.

claim: The combination of direct regulation and indirect phytohormone crosstalk may explain how a single TF can act as a node in multiple signaling processes.
source: Overall, the combination of direct regulation and indirect phytohormone crosstalk may explain how a single TF can act as a node in multiple signaling processes and integrate growth and defence responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple regulatory mechanisms observed for OsWRKY70.

claim: TrypPIs are an effective JA-dependent defence against chewing herbivores, including SSB.
source: In rice, it is well documented that TrypPIs are an effective JA-dependent defence against chewing herbivores, including SSB (Zhou et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: OsWRKY70-mediated resistance in rice to SSB is mainly due to its effect on the JA-signaling pathway.
source: These data suggest that OsWRKY70-mediated resistance in rice to SSB is mainly due to its effect on the JA-signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from JA complementation experiments showing restored resistance.

claim: Little is known about the role of GA in herbivore resistance against piercing-sucking insects.
source: On the other hand, little is known so far about the role of GA in herbivore resistance against piercing-sucking insects.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: The GA-signaling pathway plays an important role in modulating resistance in rice to BPH in addition to its regulation of plant growth.
source: These data demonstrate that the GA-signaling pathway plays an important role in modulating resistance in rice to BPH in addition to its regulation of plant growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with GA mutants and GA complementation experiments.

claim: GA may directly regulate the BPH defence response.
source: GA-modulated BPH resistance in rice may occur via two mechanisms. One is that GA directly regulates the BPH defence response.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known GA functions.

claim: GA can positively modulate the pathogen-related PBZ1 gene.
source: It has been reported that GA can positively modulate the pathogen-related PBZ1 gene (Tanaka et al., 2006) and cell modification (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: GA can positively modulate cell modification.
source: It has been reported that GA can positively modulate the pathogen-related PBZ1 gene (Tanaka et al., 2006) and cell modification (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The rigidity of the cell wall is important for resistance to BPH phloem-feeding.
source: The rigidity of the cell wall is important for resistance to BPH phloem-feeding.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: GA can directly elicit plant growth, which may enhance the tolerance of rice to BPH.
source: Moreover, GA can directly elicit the plant growth, which may enhance the tolerance of rice to BPH.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known GA functions.

claim: GA may indirectly regulate BPH resistance by eliciting SA and ROS pathways via GA-GID1-DELLA complex.
source: Another possibility is that GA indirectly regulates BPH resistance by eliciting SA and ROS pathways, both of which have been reported to be involved in resistance of rice to BPH (Zhou et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2011), via GA-GID1-DELLA complex (Navarro et al., 2008; Alonso-Ramírez et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known GA signaling mechanisms and BPH resistance pathways.

claim: SA and ROS pathways have been reported to be involved in resistance of rice to BPH.
source: Another possibility is that GA indirectly regulates BPH resistance by eliciting SA and ROS pathways, both of which have been reported to be involved in resistance of rice to BPH (Zhou et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2011), via GA-GID1-DELLA complex (Navarro et al., 2008; Alonso-Ramírez et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several elements of the rice defense signaling cascade have divergent effects on SSB and BPH.
source: Thus far, several other elements of the rice defense signaling cascade, including JA (Zhou et al., 2009), OsERF3 (Lu et al., 2011), and ethylene (Lu et al., 2014) have also been shown to have similar divergent effects on SSB and BPH, suggesting distinct resistance strategies of rice plants against these two herbivores.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rice plants have distinct resistance strategies against SSB and BPH.
source: Thus far, several other elements of the rice defense signaling cascade, including JA (Zhou et al., 2009), OsERF3 (Lu et al., 2011), and ethylene (Lu et al., 2014) have also been shown to have similar divergent effects on SSB and BPH, suggesting distinct resistance strategies of rice plants against these two herbivores.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that multiple defense components have opposite effects on the two herbivores.

claim: The main reason for the divergent signaling, response and resistance to SSB and BPH is their different feeding habits.
source: The main reason for the divergent signaling, response and resistance to the two herbivores might be their different feeding habits.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known differences in herbivore feeding modes.

claim: Resistance mechanisms against phloem-feeders differ substantially from mechanisms against chewing herbivores.
source: Resistance mechanisms against phloem-feeders are well documented to differ substantially from mechanisms against chewing herbivores (Bostock, 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OsWRKY70 plays a key role in defence prioritization.
source: In summary, our experiments provide evidence for a key role of OsWRKY70 in defence prioritization and illustrate that reducing growth via GA signaling opens the door to secondary infection by non-target herbivores.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing OsWRKY70's role in regulating both defense and growth.

claim: Reducing growth via GA signaling opens the door to secondary infection by non-target herbivores.
source: In summary, our experiments provide evidence for a key role of OsWRKY70 in defence prioritization and illustrate that reducing growth via GA signaling opens the door to secondary infection by non-target herbivores.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing increased BPH susceptibility in GA-deficient lines.

claim: When attacked by SSB, rice plants recognize signals derived from the herbivore and activate OsMPK3 and OsMPK6.
source: When attacked by a chewing herbivore such as SSB, rice plants will recognize signals derived from the herbivore and activate OsMPK3 and OsMPK6.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about MAPK activation in response to herbivory.

claim: Activated OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 elicit OsWRKY70.
source: The activated OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 then elicit OsWRKY70, which subsequently activates the JA- and ET-signaling pathways, resulting in the production of defence compounds such as TrypPIs and an increase in plant resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing reduced OsWRKY70 expression in MAPK silenced lines.

claim: OsWRKY70 activates the JA- and ET-signaling pathways.
source: The activated OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 then elicit OsWRKY70, which subsequently activates the JA- and ET-signaling pathways, resulting in the production of defence compounds such as TrypPIs and an increase in plant resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by hormone measurements showing increased JA and ET in overexpression lines.

claim: Activation of JA- and ET-signaling pathways results in the production of defence compounds such as TrypPIs and an increase in plant resistance.
source: The activated OsMPK3 and OsMPK6 then elicit OsWRKY70, which subsequently activates the JA- and ET-signaling pathways, resulting in the production of defence compounds such as TrypPIs and an increase in plant resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by TrypPI activity assays and herbivore performance assays.

claim: The activation of OsWRKY70 decreases the production of GAs.
source: Simultaneously, the activation of OsWRKY70 decreases the production of GAs, which inhibits plant growth and thus prioritizes defence overgrowth and leads to increased susceptibility to BPH.
evidence: The claim is supported by GA measurements showing decreased GA in overexpression lines.

claim: Decreased GA production inhibits plant growth and prioritizes defence over growth.
source: Simultaneously, the activation of OsWRKY70 decreases the production of GAs, which inhibits plant growth and thus prioritizes defence overgrowth and leads to increased susceptibility to BPH.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations and GA complementation experiments.

claim: Decreased GA production leads to increased susceptibility to BPH.
source: Simultaneously, the activation of OsWRKY70 decreases the production of GAs, which inhibits plant growth and thus prioritizes defence overgrowth and leads to increased susceptibility to BPH.
evidence: The claim is supported by BPH performance assays on GA-deficient lines and GA complementation experiments.

claim: The transcriptional modulation of hormonal networks allows plants to mount an appropriate defence program.
source: Through these results, our study illustrates that the transcriptional modulation of hormonal networks allows plants to mount an appropriate defence program.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OsWRKY70 regulates multiple hormone pathways to coordinate defense responses.

claim: Prioritizing defence over growth leads to significant resistance trade-offs, which may constrain plant resistance breeding.
source: At the same time, however, prioritizing defence over growth leads to significant resistance trade-offs, which may constrain plant resistance breeding and favor the evolution of herbivore-specific responses in plants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that defense prioritization leads to increased susceptibility to non-target herbivores.

claim: Prioritizing defence over growth may favor the evolution of herbivore-specific responses in plants.
source: At the same time, however, prioritizing defence over growth leads to significant resistance trade-offs, which may constrain plant resistance breeding and favor the evolution of herbivore-specific responses in plants.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on evolutionary considerations of resistance trade-offs.
